meta.program: Internal Bridges · Thrive Thursday · Anchor's Edge · Vanderbilt
meta.audience: All Vanderbilt staff in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm; no management experience assumed. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; November is the Transfer Portal in Practice month, and this session builds its human network.
meta.roomSetup: Virtual, instructor led: camera on, deck link in chat, breakouts of 2 available. Learners follow on their own screens via the welcome-slide link or QR. Nothing typed into the deck is saved or sent.
meta.postSession: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did the bridge move on your card happen? What did you learn that you could never have guessed? Which bridge is next?' Count of sent invites and follow-ups is the Level 3 metric for the month.

full.description: The full 45-minute virtual session: every interaction runs live, breakouts run in pairs, and the capstone gets read-alouds. The per-section minutes on each slide sum to 45 including transitions.

core.description: The 30-minute slot: agenda and core-idea slides pass in stride, breakouts become solo passes with chat share-outs, debriefs shrink to one voice. Never cut the section interactions or the capstone.

meta.framework: ATD facilitator-guide structure: per module SAY / DO / ASK (with anticipated responses) / DEBRIEF / TRANSITION, plus preparation checklists, materials, contingencies, and a tough-questions bank.
materials: Meeting platform with screen share and breakout rooms; deck link ready to paste in chat
Facilitator machine with the facilitator edition open; notifications off
Learners on their own devices with the learner link
Chat open for share-outs; the capstone copy button pastes there cleanly

weekBefore: Run the learner edition start to finish and do every interaction honestly; you will demo at least one live.
Read this month's theme page on the Anchor's Edge dashboard so the goal tie-in is fluent.
Send the invite with the learner link and one line on what to bring.
dayBefore: Test screen share with the facilitator edition; confirm the notes rail is readable.
Open the learner link on a second device; the QR must land there.
Run the section interactions once so you can drive them without reading.
thirtyMinBefore: Welcome slide up as people join; link pasted in chat.
Close every other tab; silence the machine.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: Someone says they have no time for networking
contingencies.then: Do the math aloud: one 20-minute coffee and two 2-minute follow-ups a month is under half an hour. Compare that with the cost of starting every search, project, and question from cold.

contingencies.if: A participant wants to network only for a specific job they are chasing
contingencies.then: Honor the goal and widen the frame: a live application is Portal work, and a navigator can help today. Bridges are the long game that means the next opportunity finds them.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't this just politics with better branding?
toughQuestions.a: Politics is managing impressions; this is trading genuine curiosity. The test is simple: if the other person got nothing from the exchange, it was politics. A good coffee leaves them feeling interesting and you knowing more. Both sides gained.

toughQuestions.q: I'm an introvert. Is there a version of this for me?
toughQuestions.a: This is the introvert version: one person, twenty minutes, prepared questions, and listening as the main event. The model that requires working a room is the one we threw out in section one.

toughQuestions.q: What if I invite someone senior and they ignore me?
toughQuestions.a: Expect some silence; senior calendars eat invites. A specific, bounded, curious invite lands better than you fear, and one gentle nudge after two weeks is fine. After that, pick another door; curiosity has plenty of targets.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Thursday, 45 minutes on networking without the ick. Bring one team at Vanderbilt you are genuinely curious about. That is the only homework. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the bridge move happen? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did the invite or follow-up on your card go out? 2) What did you learn that you could never have guessed? 3) Which bridge is next?

sections.title: Welcome / QR
sections.purpose: Get everyone into the deck on their own screen and set the tone: 45 minutes, live, hands on.
sections.say: Welcome to Thrive Thursday. Scan the code or click the link in chat so this session runs on your screen too. Forty-five minutes, one focus: Networking without the ick: building internal bridges.
facilitate: Slide up as people join; link pasted in chat every few minutes.
State the norm once: type into your own screen, nothing you enter is saved or sent.
sections.watchFor: People lurking without the deck open. The interactions only land if the deck is on their screen.
sections.transition: Before the topic, thirty seconds on why Vanderbilt is asking for this hour.

sections.title: Why we're here
sections.purpose: Anchor the session in the Chancellor's charge and name the goal this month serves, inside one minute.
sections.say: One sentence from the Chancellor sits over everything we do: Vanderbilt will define the great university of the 21st Century and be it. Radical Collaboration is a chancellor-level bet that Vanderbilt's best work happens across boundaries, and every bridge between departments is that bet paying off at human scale. This month serves Goal 1, Talent Marketplace & Transfer Portal.
facilitate: Read the mission line slowly, once; name the goal, once.
No discussion here; the whole slide is under a minute.
sections.transition: Here is what you will be able to do in 45 minutes.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.purpose: Set the contract for the session in about a minute; this slide is also the roadmap.
sections.say: By the end of this session you will be able to: swap transactional networking for curiosity-based connecting across departments; run a 20-minute virtual coffee, from the invite to the thank-you; keep a bridge warm with small, genuine follow-ups that take two minutes. We take them in order, and each one has something to practice.
facilitate: Read the three objectives briskly; they double as the agenda.
Point at the goal chip once, then move.

sections.title: Networking without the ick
sections.say: Most people dislike the word networking, and that reaction is useful information: it is what extraction feels like from the outside. Today we practice a different version, one that runs on genuine curiosity about how other people's work actually happens. If you have a question you actually want answered, the outreach writes itself and you never need a script.
facilitate: Read the curiosity test card aloud once.
Show the in-the-room card in place of the quiz; ask in chat for one word on what makes networking feel gross.
Open the discussion: an outreach that felt gross to receive, and its curious version. Two or three voices.
Run the breakout: one team you are curious about and the question you would ask.

ask.q: Which Vanderbilt team's work are you genuinely curious about?
expect: Often a team they collaborate with but have never really met
Sometimes something completely unrelated to their role
ask.respond: Notice how easy that question was. That is the whole reframe: your curiosity already exists; networking is just letting it out of the building.

sections.debrief: The curiosity test does the filtering: a real question means the right person, and no question means the wrong one.
sections.watchFor: Self-identified introverts opting out early. Name it: this model favors them; one genuine question beats an hour of working a room.
sections.transition: Curiosity needs a container. Ours is twenty minutes long.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; run the context card and take three curiosity targets in chat.

sections.title: The 20-minute coffee
sections.purpose: Give everyone a repeatable format: the specific bounded invite and the question-led twenty minutes.
sections.say: The unit of internal networking is the 20-minute virtual coffee. Twenty minutes is short enough that a stranger says yes and long enough to actually learn something. The coffee is won or lost in the invite, though. Name the thing about their work you are curious about and cap the time; that is the whole formula. Then spend the minutes on your questions and their answers, and end when you said you would.
facilitate: Run Build the coffee; two minutes to choose both slots and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: specific bounded invite, question-led minutes.

ask.q: Why does ending at twenty minutes matter so much?
expect: It proves you meant the invite
ask.respond: It also compounds. The person who ends on time is the person whose next invite gets accepted within the hour.

sections.debrief: Specific invite, real questions, clean ending. The format is small on purpose; small is what makes it repeatable.
sections.watchFor: People drafting invites that are secretly job inquiries. Redirect to the curiosity test: the coffee is for learning, and opportunity follows on its own.
sections.transition: One good coffee is a plank. Keeping it warm is what makes it a bridge.
sections.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

sections.title: Keeping bridges warm
sections.purpose: Install the two-minute warm follow-up habit and the instincts for cadence.
sections.say: Here is where most bridges die: the coffee goes great, everyone means to stay in touch, and eleven months later it feels too late to write. The fix costs two minutes when something reminds you of them. Specific, generous, occasional. And if a bridge has already gone cold, the dormant-ties research in MIT Sloan Management Review is comforting: when people reconnected with contacts they had not spoken to in years, the advice they got often beat their current network, and the old trust was still there. Cold is recoverable. Warm is just cheaper.
facilitate: Run Call the follow-up live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, pause on the resume-after-silence pattern; ask why it lands so badly.
Run the breakout: one contact and the two-minute follow-up you could send.

ask.q: What makes the article-link follow-up in round one so effective?
ask.respond: Right. Generosity at two-minute scale is the most underpriced move in professional life. Nobody forgets the person who remembered.

sections.debrief: A warm follow-up asks for nothing. The bridge you keep warm carries opportunity later, and even a cold one can be reopened; the dormant-ties research says the trust keeps.
sections.watchFor: People turning the follow-up into a scheduled campaign. Keep it human: when you genuinely think of them, send the two minutes.
sections.transition: Quick recap, then you pick your first bridge.
sections.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.purpose: Land the one sentence the session exists to install.
sections.say: If you keep one sentence from today, this is it. Read it once, out loud: Invite with a real question, and follow up with something that asks for nothing.
facilitate: Pause two beats after reading; the word animation carries it.
sections.coreNote: Core: pass through in stride; the sentence reads itself.

sections.title: Recap quiz
sections.purpose: Score the learning while it is fresh; wrong answers are teaching moments, not failures.
sections.say: Three questions, on your own screen. Answer honestly; the explanations are where the learning sticks.
facilitate: Give the room 90 seconds to run it individually.
Ask for a show of results in chat: how many got 3 of 3?
Read out the explanation for whichever question drew the most misses.
sections.watchFor: Rushing past the why lines. The explanations carry the teaching.
sections.transition: Now point it at your real week.

sections.title: Capstone commitment
sections.purpose: Convert the session into one named, dated action per person.
sections.say: Now make it real. One bridge: a team, your genuine question, and the move you will make. Teams and roles, never names. Build the card, copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday, and take two quiet minutes to do it now.
facilitate: Two quiet minutes; everyone builds their own card.
Invite two or three volunteers to read their card aloud or paste it in chat.
Remind: copy the card somewhere you will see it this week.
sections.watchFor: Vague entries. Nudge for a name-able situation and a real date.

sections.title: Closing
sections.purpose: End with the next step and where this thread continues.
sections.say: You leave with a curiosity test and a two-minute habit that keeps bridges standing. That closes the Transfer Portal week: Monday gave managers the sending mindset, Tuesday walked the Portal end to end, and today built the bridges that carry the news. If you want more this month, the navigators are running a live Portal walkthrough and a skill-profile clinic, and the LinkedIn Learning pick is Building Your Team by Chris Croft. Next month the series takes up the Vanderbilt Manager Standard; same time, same rhythm.
facilitate: Point at the next-step card; one sentence.
